rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads the verb with a doubled tāʾ here and in thirty-one Qurʾanic places; the other readers use the lighter form.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير غير القواس ولا تيمموا بتشديد التاء فيها وفي أخواتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two readings mean the same; the doubled form restores and assimilates the dropped tāʾ, while common recitation omits one of the two tāʾs for ease.
rows.anchor: كلاهما بمعنى واحد كأن ابن كثير رد الحرف الساقط في القراءة الأخرى وأدغم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tayammum means deliberately intending or aiming at something; Khifaf and al-Aʿshā use it this way, as do related forms for intending or being a target.
rows.anchor: اللغة: التيمم التعمد قال خفاف:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khabīth means the defective or inferior thing; the dross expelled from silver and iron is called khabath, whose root sense is badness.
rows.anchor: والخبيث الرديء من كل شيء وخبث الفضة والحديد ما نفاه الكير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In trade, igmāḍ means accepting a reduced price for a defect; its root concerns concealment, with related senses of closing the eyes and sleep.
rows.anchor: والإغماض في البيع الحط من الثمن لعيب فيه وذلك لإخفاء بعض الثمن

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ construes an in illā an tughmiḍū as conditional: if you show some forbearance, you will take it, so the hamza is kasra.
rows.anchor: الأصل في أن تغمضوا أن مكسورة الهمزة لأن الكلام في معنى الجزاء

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The leading grammarians reject the conditional analysis: an here is a verbal noun, meaning you would take it only through your forbearance.
rows.anchor: وأنكر ذلك المحققون قالوا أن هذه التي بمعنى المصدر نحو أن تأتيني خير لك

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: One reported occasion is people donating assets from pre-Islamic usury; they were forbidden to give these and commanded to give lawful, wholesome wealth.
rows.anchor: روي عن أبي عبد الله ع أنها نزلت في أقوام لهم أموال من ربا الجاهلية

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Another occasion concerns people putting poor-quality dried dates into the charity dates; this is reported from ʿAlī, al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib, al-Ḥasan, and Qatāda.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنها نزلت في قوم كانوا يأتون بالحشف فيدخلونه في تمر الصدقة عن علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage completes the prior discussion of spending by describing the gift and its recipient: believers are told to give charity while preserving it from invalidation by reproach or harm.
rows.anchor: لما تقدم ذكر الإنفاق وبيان صفة المنفق وأنه يجب أن ينوي بالصدقة التقرب

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: One explanation of good earnings is lawful income acquired through trade, reported from Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid.
rows.anchor: من حلال ما كسبتم بالتجارة عن ابن مسعود ومجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the phrase as the best and finest of what one has earned.
rows.anchor: وقيل من خياره وجياده ونظيره قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding phrase is illustrated by the command to spend what one loves in order to attain righteousness.
rows.anchor: لن تنالوا البر حتى تنفقوا مما تحبون

rows.speaker: عبيد بن رفاعة
rows.claim: A report from ʿUbayd b. Rifāʿa quotes the Prophet warning that merchants are sinners except those who are God-fearing, dutiful, truthful, and charitable.
rows.anchor: روي عن عبيد بن رفاعة قال خرج علينا رسول الله

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is also quoted as saying that nine tenths of provision comes from trade and the remainder from seafaring.
rows.anchor: تسعة أعشار الرزق في التجارة والجزء الباقي في السابياء

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports the Prophet saying that the best food a person eats is from his own earning, and that his child is part of his earning.
rows.anchor: وروت عائشة عنه أنه قال

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report through Saʿīd b. ʿUmayr quotes the Prophet saying that a person best earns through work by hand and every sound sale.
rows.anchor: سئل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أي كسب الرجل أطيب

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī warns that anyone trading without knowledge becomes entangled in usury again and again.
rows.anchor: علي ع: من اتجر بغير علم

rows.speaker: عبيدة السلماني
rows.claim: One view makes the command refer specifically to obligatory alms; this is attributed to ʿUbayda al-Salmānī and al-Ḥasan.
rows.anchor: فقيل هذا أمر بالنفقة في الزكاة عن عبيدة السلماني والحسن

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī limits it to voluntary charity, since obligatory alms have a set value owed as a debt if underpaid, and even entirely poor-quality wealth may be used for zakat.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو في الصدقة المتطوع بها لأن المفروض من الصدقة له مقدار من القيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers a general command covering obligatory and voluntary spending in every good cause; it also indicates that charity from earned lawful wealth brings greater reward because it costs more.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو الأصح أنه يدخل فيه الفرائض والنوافل والمراد به الإنفاق في سبيل الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The produce from the earth means crops and fruits subject to zakat, which should also be given.
rows.anchor: من الغلات والثمار مما يجب فيه الزكاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Do not deliberately select inferior wealth, whether earned or grown; some interpret khabīth as unlawful wealth, but the first interpretation fits the comparison to something accepted only reluctantly.
rows.anchor: ولا تيمموا الخبيث منه تنفقون

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: One explanation of accepting it only with igmāḍ is that a creditor would take such an item from a debtor only by lenient accommodation.
rows.anchor: الإغماض ها هنا المساهلة عن البراء بن عازب

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Another explanation is that one would accept it only by discounting its price; al-Ḥasan, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and al-Zajjāj are cited for this sense.
rows.anchor: إلا أن تحطوا من الثمن فيه عن الحسن وابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is independent of charity yet worthy of praise; hamīd may mean deserving praise, eliciting praise through gifts, or praising and rewarding donors, with the last fitting this context best.
rows.anchor: أي مستحق للحمد على نعمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamīd suits this verse better than ḥalīm: after commanding the best earnings, God says He needs none of them yet praises those who obey and rewards their giving.
rows.anchor: حميد بهذا الموضع أليق من حليم كما أن حلميا بالآية المتقدمة أليق من حميد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faqr means need, opposite of wealth; related forms describe poverty, the back vertebrae, a calamity that breaks them, and a mount lowered for riding.
rows.anchor: الفقر الحاجة وهو ضد الغنى والفقر لغة فيه يقال أفقره الله إفقارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waʿd, promise, can refer to good or evil when qualified, but when unqualified or left vague it denotes good; waʿīd is specifically a threat of evil.
rows.anchor: والفرق بين الوعد والوعيد أن الوعيد في الشر خاصة والوعد يصلح بالتقييد

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā glosses faḥshāʾ as sins; the miser is called fāḥish because refusing guests and petitioners is offensive, as illustrated by poetry of Ṭarafa and Kaʿb.
rows.anchor: قال علي بن عيسى الفحشاء المعاصي وإنما سمي البخيل فاحشا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan frightens people that giving to good causes or giving their best wealth will make them poor; one view specifies payment of zakat.
rows.anchor: بالنفقة في وجوه البر وبإنفاق الجيد من المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's command to faḥshāʾ means sins and abandoning obedience, or spending from inferior wealth; that is disobedience and can sever ties when the wealthy withhold from needy kin and neighbors.
rows.anchor: أي بالمعاصي وترك الطاعات وقيل بالإنفاق من الردى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises that giving the best wealth will cover sins and pardon punishment, replace the gift with better provision, and increase His bounty.
rows.anchor: أن يستر عليكم ويصفح عن عقوبتكم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās divides the promises into two from God—pardon and increased provision—and two from Satan—fear of poverty and an order to sin.
rows.anchor: اثنان من الله واثنان من الشيطان فاللذان من الله المغفرة على المعاصي

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, with a similar report from Abū ʿAbd Allāh, describes one prompting from Satan and one from the angel: Satan urges poverty and sin, while the angel urges giving and forbids sin.
rows.anchor: للشيطان لمة وللملك لمة وروي مثله عن أبي عبد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's breadth means that giving does not harm Him or diminish His stores; He knows who deserves a gift.
rows.anchor: واسع معناه يعطي عن سعة بمعنى إن عطيته لا تضره ولا تنقص خزائنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To enrich or avail someone means to ward off harm that otherwise would have reached him; wealth is whatever removes need, whether money, rank, or companions.
rows.anchor: يقال أغنى عنه إذا دفع عنه ضررا لولاه لنزل به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers' wealth and children are named because they are people's chief supports and most prized possessions; if these cannot help, lesser things are even less likely to help.
rows.anchor: لأن هذين معتمد الخلق وأعز الأشياء عليهم فإذا لم يغنيا عن الإنسان شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A companion is fundamentally one who remains with another, though the word can denote those who dwell with, own, follow, or learn from someone; the additions differ in sense.
rows.anchor: وأصل المصاحبة الملازمة والنار أصله من النور

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The spending may refer generally to all the charity and expenditure of disbelievers in worldly life; other views specify support for fighting the Messenger, Abū Sufyān's spending at Badr and Uḥud, or Jewish commoners' support of scholars.
rows.anchor: قيل هو ما ينفقون على الكفار في عداوة الرسول وقيل هو ما أنفقه أبو سفيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison omits the word for destruction: their spending is like the destruction of a crop by a severe cold wind, and the ellipsis is signaled by the verse's end.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية حذف وتقديره مثل إهلاك ما ينفقون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ṣirr is interpreted as severe cold by Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and others; Ibn ʿAbbās also reports the alternative of a deadly hot simoom.
rows.anchor: قيل برد شديد عن ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة وجماعة وقيل السموم الحارة القاتلة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains ṣirr as the sound of a flame carried by the wind, while another possibility is the crashing noise of the cold north wind.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج الصر صوت لهب النار التي كانت في تلك الريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The crop owners are described as having wronged themselves through sins; another view says they planted in the wrong place or season, so the wind destroyed the crop as correction.
rows.anchor: فظلمهم اقتضى هلك حرثهم عقوبة لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God did not wrong them by destroying the crop, or by killing and capturing them, because their wrongdoing and disbelief made them deserve it.
rows.anchor: في إهلاك زرعهم لأنهما استحقوا ذلك بظلمهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the yāʾ reading, those who withhold are the subject and the understood first object is their withholding; huwa separates the subject from the predicate. The tāʾ reading addresses the Prophet and omits the object meaning their withholding.
rows.anchor: فمن قرأ يحسبن بالياء فالذين يبخلون فاعل يحسبن والمفعول الأول محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bukhul is withholding what is due; its lexical root also connotes difficulty in giving.
rows.anchor: والبخل هو منع الواجب لأنه توعد عليه وذم به وأصله في اللغة المشقة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read the end of the verse with yāʾ, referring to those who withhold; the other readers address the audience with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ويعقوب يعملون بالياء كناية عن الذين يبخلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke concerns people who withhold the obligatory rights from wealth God has given them; such stinginess is bad for them, not good as they suppose.
rows.anchor: فيبخلون بإخراج الحقوق الواجبة فيها ذلك البخل هو خيرا لهم بل هو شر لهم

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: One interpretation says withheld wealth will become a collar around its owner's neck; the verse concerns zakat refusers, as reported from Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, al-Shaʿbī, and others.
rows.anchor: قيل يجعل ما بخل به من المال طوقا في عنقه والآية نزلت في مانعي الزكاة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that a man who fails to pay zakat will have a serpent placed around his neck on Judgment Day, then recites the verse.
rows.anchor: ما من رجل لا يؤدي الزكاة إلا جعل في عنقه شجاع يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is also reported to describe a relative who withholds God's bounty: God will bring a serpent from Hell, which will lick its tongue and encircle the miser.
rows.anchor: وتلا هذه الآية، وقيل معناه

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī interprets the punishment as a collar of fire around the miser's neck on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه يجعل في عنقه يوم القيامة طوقا من نار عن النخعي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the miser will be made to produce on Judgment Day the wealth he withheld.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه يكلفون يوم القيامة أن يأتوا بما بخلوا به من أموالهم عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī reads the punishment as the withheld wealth becoming a collar used to torment its owner, like the heated treasure in 9:35.
rows.anchor: فمعناه أنه يجعل طوقا فيعذب بها عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: ابن مسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Muslim says the harm returns on the miser and becomes a collar, as in the image of each person's deed fastened to his neck in 17:13; Arabs can use neck or throat for the whole body.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه أنه يعود عليهم وباله فيصير طوقا لأعناقهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report from Ibn ʿAbbās takes the verse to concern those who concealed the description of Muhammad, with God's bounty referring to the Torah containing that description; the first view better fits the context.
rows.anchor: ويروى عن ابن عباس أيضا أن المراد بالآية الذين يبخلون ببيان صفة محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God inheriting heaven and earth means all creatures die and every owner's property ends while God's ownership remains forever; this urges people not to cling to wealth that will pass away.
rows.anchor: يموت من في السماوات والأرض ويبقى تعالى هو جل جلاله لم يزل ولا يزال

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: The verse connects to the prior discussion because, like their stinginess about jihad, they were stingy about spending and zakat; another view says they concealed Muhammad's prophethood.
rows.anchor: الوجه في اتصال الآية بما قبلها هو أنهم كما بخلوا بالجهاد بخلوا بالإنفاق

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: The supplication for fulfillment of God's promise is an expression of submission, pleading, and worship, as in the prayer for judgment in 21:112; ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā and al-Jubbāʾī choose this answer.
rows.anchor: أن ذلك على وجه الانقطاع إلى الله والتضرع له والتعبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second answer treats the prayer as declarative rather than an expression of doubt: the believers know God will fulfill His promise and ask to be gathered with the righteous and spared disgrace.
rows.anchor: أن الكلام خرج مخرج المسألة والمراد الخبر أي توفنا مع الأبرار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third answer says they ask to be included among those granted the promised honor by the messengers, without claiming they personally deserve that honor.
rows.anchor: معناه السؤال والدعاء بأن يجعلهم ممن أتاهم ما وعدهم من الكرامة

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī's preferred answer is that they ask God to hasten the promised victory over unbelieving enemies and the triumph of truth; the promise had no set date, and the context supports this reading.
rows.anchor: وهو اختيار الطبري وقال الآية مختصة بمن هاجر من أصحاب النبي

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم البلخي
rows.claim: Abū al-Qāsim al-Balkhī also gestures toward the interpretation that the prayer seeks an earlier victory for the emigrants among the Prophet's Companions.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا أومى أبو القاسم البلخي أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance in its fullest sense is regret for a wrong coupled with resolve not to repeat it; another definition requires only regret and resolve not to repeat an equally grave wrong.
rows.anchor: أصل التوبة الرجوع وحقيقتها الندم على القبيح مع العزم على أن لا يعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿtadnā may derive from aʿdadnā with tāʾ substituting for dāl, or may be a verb formed from ʿatād, equipment; the latter is illustrated by ʿAdī b. al-Riqāʿ's poetry.
rows.anchor: هو أفعلنا من العتاد وهو العدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about those who die is grammatically genitive by coordination with the earlier phrase, with an implied repetition of “nor for.”
rows.anchor: موضع الذين يموتون جر بكونه عطفا على قوله للذين يعملون السوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author defines accepted repentance as available only to people who sin in ignorance and repent soon; innamā both excludes and affirms, so this repentance is for that class alone.
rows.anchor: ولفظة إنما يتضمن النفي والإثبات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and a report from Abū ʿAbd Allāh take every sin as done in ignorance, even deliberately, because sinning risks oneself against God; Joseph likewise called his brothers ignorant in 12:89.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وعطاء ومجاهد وقتادة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the sinner acts in ignorance because he does not fully know the punishment entailed, unlike knowledge that is certain and immediate.
rows.anchor: أن معنى قوله بجهالة أنهم لا يعلمون كنه ما فيه من العقوبة

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says people may sin because they mistakenly believe the act lawful or fail to reason through its ugliness; al-Rummānī rejects this because it contradicts exegetical consensus and would deny repentance to those aware of their sin.
rows.anchor: الجبائي، وضعف الرماني هذا القول لأنه

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya and Qatāda say the Companions agreed that every sin a person commits counts as ignorance.
rows.anchor: أبو العالية، وقتادة: أجمعت الصحابة على أن كل ذنب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says choosing fleeting pleasure over lasting pleasure is ignorance in the act of choice.
rows.anchor: إنما قال الجهالة لأنهم في اختيارهم اللذة الفانية على اللذة الباقية جهال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Soon” means before death, since the span remaining before death is short; repentance remains accepted until the person knows death is certain.
rows.anchor: يتوبون قبل الموت لأن ما بين الإنسان وبين الموت قريب

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Ibn ʿUmar define “soon” as the period before a person sees death approaching.
rows.anchor: الحسن والضحاك وابن عمر: القريب ما لم يعاين الموت

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī defines the accepted period as health, before illness and death.
rows.anchor: السدي: هو ما دام في الصحة قبل المرض والموت

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: When asked what if someone repeatedly returns to sin and repents, ʿAlī says God forgives him, even if asked how long; he answers until Satan himself is bewitched.
rows.anchor: روي عن أمير المؤمنين ع أنه قيل له فإن عاد وتاب مرارا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: In the final sermon, the Prophet reportedly promises acceptance for repentance begun a year, a month, a day, or an hour before death, even when the soul reaches the throat.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في آخر خطبة خطبها

rows.speaker: عبادة بن الصامت
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī transmits the same Prophetic report through ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit, ending that repentance is accepted before the death rattle.
rows.anchor: وروى الثعلبي بإسناده عن عبادة بن الصامت عن النبي هذا الخبر بعينه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reports a divine exchange: Iblīs vows not to leave Adam's descendants until their souls depart, and God vows not to bar repentance until death's rattle.
rows.anchor: بإسناده عن الحسن قال: قال رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepts the repentance of those just described and knows what benefits His servants, acting wisely toward them.
rows.anchor: أي يقبل توبتهم { وكان الله عليما } بمصالح العباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accepted repentance does not extend to persistent sinners who delay until death's signs and hope of life have ended; at that point they say they repent now.
rows.anchor: أي المعاصي ويصرون عليها ويسوفون التوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes agree the verse concerns sinful Muslims, apart from a report from al-Rabīʿ that it concerns hypocrites; the author rejects that because hypocrites are unbelievers, separately named in the next clause.
rows.anchor: وأجمع أهل التأويل على أن هذه تناولت عصاة أهل الإسلام إلا ما روي عن الربيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelievers named afterward are those who die in unbelief and regret only after death; God has prepared for them painful punishment.
rows.anchor: ومعناه وليست التوبة أيضا للذين يموتون على الكفر ثم يندمون بعد الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance at death is invalid because the dying person is compelled to choose good and abandon evil, outside moral responsibility and thus outside the conditions of repentance; the afterlife is similarly beyond obligation.
rows.anchor: لأنه يكون العبد هناك ملجأ إلى فعل الحسنات وترك القبائح فيكون خارجا عن حد التكليف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “prepared a painful punishment” does not prove that sinful believers who die unrepentant must be punished: it can mean they merit Hell, may refer to the nearer unbelievers, or describe what justice would impose absent divine pardon.
rows.anchor: إن معنى إعداد العذاب لهم إنما هو خلق النار التي هي مصيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to forgive lesser sins whoever God wills applies only to monotheist believers who die with an unrepented major sin; the righteous, repentant, and unbelievers are not in that class.
rows.anchor: المشيئة فيه إلا المؤمنين من أهل الكبائر الذين يموتون قبل التوبة

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ claims this verse was abrogated by the promise that God forgives lesser sins for whom He wills in 4:48 and 4:116.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع: إن الآية منسوخة بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects abrogation because this verse states a report about what God has prepared, and reports cannot be abrogated as legal commands can.
rows.anchor: وارد مورد الخبر، فلا يجوز النسخ فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads the temporal phrase with wāw as al-ghudwa throughout the Qurʾan; the other readers read al-ghadāh with alif.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر بالغدوة والعشي في كل القرآن بواو والباقون بالغداة بالألف

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī argues al-ghadāh is preferable because it is an indefinite noun that can take the article, whereas ghudwa is a proper name and does not become indefinite; the grammarians' reports also support ghudāh.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: الوجه الغداة لأنها تستعمل نكرة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: The reading ghudwa is also defended: al-Khalīl allows it as a temporal adverb like ḍuḥwa, and other time names can appear definite without the article.
rows.anchor: ووجه قراءة ابن عامر أن سيبويه قال زعم الخليل أنه يجوز أن تقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then you would expel them” answers the preceding negation, and “then you would be among the wrongdoers” is subjunctive as the result of the prohibition not to expel.
rows.anchor: فتطردهم جواب للنفي في قوله ما عليك من حسابهم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports Quraysh leaders passing the Prophet while he sat with poor Muslims—Ṣuhayb, Khabbāb, Bilāl, and ʿAmmār—and asking him to expel them so the leaders might follow him.
rows.anchor: روى الثعلبي بإسناده عن عبد الله بن مسعود قال مر الملأ من قريش على رسول الله

rows.speaker: سلمان
rows.claim: Salmān and Khabbāb say the verse was revealed concerning them.
rows.anchor: وقال سلمان وخباب: فينا نزلت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report describes al-Aqraʿ b. Ḥābis, ʿUyayna b. Ḥiṣn, and other leaders disparaging the poor believers and asking the Prophet to dismiss them when Arab delegations came; he agrees, but Gabriel reveals the prohibition and the Prophet tears up their proposed written pledge.
rows.anchor: جاء الأقرع بن حابس التميمي وعيينه بن حصين الفزاري وذووهم من المؤلفة قلوبهم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: After the revelation, the Prophet tells the believers that their Lord has prescribed mercy, then quotes God's instruction to keep patient company with them and says he will live and die among them.
rows.anchor: فكنا نقعد معه فإذا أراد أن يقوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God forbids His Messenger from acceding to the polytheists' demand to expel the believers who worship Him at dawn and evening.
rows.anchor: ثم نهى سبحانه رسوله عليه واله السلام عن إجابة المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited words from Noah say that their reckoning rests with the Lord alone, supporting the interpretation that God alone will judge the believers deeds.
rows.anchor: إن حسابهم إلا على ربي لو تشعرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The polytheists despised the poor believers because of their poverty and devotion, wanting them set below themselves in the gathering; the verse rebuts this social contempt.
rows.anchor: وهذا لأن المشركين أزدروهم لفقرهم وحاجتهم إلى الأعمال الدينية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation says the Prophet is not responsible for believers livelihood, so poverty is no reason to tire of them and expel them.
rows.anchor: ما عليك من حساب رزقهم من شيء فتملهم وتطردهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God provides both the poor believers and the Prophet, so neither party depends on the other for provision.
rows.anchor: أي ليس رزقهم عليك ولا رزقك عليهم وإنما يرزقك وإياهم الله

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets the warning as saying the Prophet would wrong the believers if he expelled them; Ibn ʿAbbās says such expulsion would harm the Prophet himself through disobedience.
rows.anchor: لهم بطردهم عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says the warning is severe because the Prophet had considered preferring wealthy leaders to attract their followers, intending good rather than contempt for the poor, but God forbade it.
rows.anchor: عظم الأمر في هذا على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وخوف الدخول في جملة الظالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tests wealthy leaders through poor believers: a proud notable may refuse faith when a poorer person has preceded him, lest he lose precedence.
rows.anchor: ابتلينا هؤلاء الرؤساء من قريش بالموالي فإذا نظر الشريف إلى الوضيع قد آمن قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is described as testing though He needs no test because He treats people as a tester would; the outcome clause means the affair resulted in their asking whether God favored these believers.
rows.anchor: وهو لا يحتاج إلى الاختبار لأنه عاملهم معاملة المختبر

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī interprets the test as the difficult obligation imposed on Arab nobles to believe and give precedence to those who believed first; the clause lets believers accept the Prophet's honor toward them rather than denying God's favor.
rows.anchor: المعنى في فتنا شددنا التكليف على إشراف العرب بأن أمرناهم بالإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in the outcome clause marks consequence: God acted so they might be patient and grateful, and their question was the eventual outcome.
rows.anchor: هذه لام العاقبة المعنى فعلنا هذا ليصبروا ويشكروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question whether God knows the grateful is a confirming question, as illustrated by Jarīr poetry.
rows.anchor: هذا استفهام تقرير أي إنه كذلك كقول جرير

none: This segment only contains the conclusion already recorded from its surrounding passage?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author defines asking as requesting an answer and enquiring as requesting information; qasas means successive narration, and related words refer to following one another in cutting, storytelling, retaliation, and offsetting a debt.
rows.anchor: السؤال طلب الجواب بأدائه في الكلام كما أن الاستخبار طلب الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mīzān means comparing two things to reveal their measure and extends metaphorically to poetic meter and measured speech; truth is putting things where wisdom requires, while weight is downward force and lightness upward force.
rows.anchor: والوزن في اللغة هو مقابلة أحد الشيئين بالآخر حتى يظهر مقداره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ in the transition to questioning links events that are distant in time as if near, a usage also found in verses about the approaching Hour and human creation.
rows.anchor: الفاء في قوله فلنسألن عاطفة جملة وإنما دخلت الفاء وهي موجبة للتعقيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questioned parties are the peoples who received messengers, about their response, and the messengers, about delivering God's message; although God already knows, the questioning warns people to prepare.
rows.anchor: فيُسأل هؤلاء عن الإبلاغ ويسأل أولئك عن الامتثال وهو تعالى وإن كان عالما

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the nations will be questioned reproachfully and the prophets as witnesses to the truth.
rows.anchor: سؤال توبيخ والأنبياء يسألون سؤال شهادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questioning demonstrates that God sent messengers and removed excuses, confirms that unbelievers earned punishment, increases the faithful's joy and unbelievers' grief, and serves as a warning that benefits those who hear it.
rows.anchor: أن يعلم الخلائق أنه سبحانه أرسل الرسل وأزاح العلة وأنه لا يظلم أحدا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God recounts events with full knowledge, while their record speaks as in 45:29; “not absent” means nothing about them was hidden from His knowledge.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: معنى قوله فلنقصن عليهم بعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says God was never absent from the messengers' delivery or the peoples' response; the wording underscores that nothing is hidden from Him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عن الرسل فيما بلغوا وعن الأمم فيما أجابوا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Balkhī understand the balance as justice in the afterlife, where no one is wronged.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد والضحاك وهو قول البلخي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and al-Jubbāʾī say God sets up a real balance with a tongue and two pans to weigh good and bad deeds.
rows.anchor: أن الله ينصب ميزانا له لسان وكفتان يوم القيامة فتوزن به أعمال العباد

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: One proposed account is that the records of deeds themselves are weighed, reported from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar and others.
rows.anchor: فقيل توزن صحائف الأعمال عن عبد الله بن عمر وجماعة

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī offers the possibility that signs of good and bad deeds appear in the balance's pans and are seen by people.
rows.anchor: في الكفتين فيراها الناس عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another view from Ibn ʿAbbās says good deeds are shown in a beautiful form and bad deeds in an ugly form.
rows.anchor: للحسنات صورة حسنة وللسيئات صورة سيئة عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr says the believer and unbeliever themselves are weighed; a physically huge man may weigh less than a gnat's wing.
rows.anchor: توزن نفس المؤمن والكافر عن عبيد بن عمير قال يؤتى بالرجل العظيم الجثة

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim reads weighing as the believer's high standing and the unbeliever's humiliation, like the declaration that they will have no weight in 18:105.
rows.anchor: أن المراد بالوزن ظهور مقدار المؤمن في العظم ومقدار الكافر في الذلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the metaphorical justice reading, followed by the literal scale, since Arabs call apt words and deeds “weighed”; he also considers the literal view supported by transmitted reports and the apparent wording.
rows.anchor: وأحسن الأقوال القول الأول وبعده الثاني وإنما قلنا ذلك لأنه اشتهر من العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poetic example speaks of measured, sound speech, including indirect expression; weighing may mean that something stands in the mind as equal to its comparison.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه من اللحن الذي هو سرعة الفهم والفطنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawāzīn is plural because each kind of worship may have its own scale, or each scale may correspond to a category of a person's deeds; a report says prayer is a scale.
rows.anchor: إنما جمع الموازين لأنه يجوز أن يكون لكل نوع من أنواع الطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those whose scales are heavy succeed by winning God's reward.
rows.anchor: أي الفائزون بثواب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those with light scales lose themselves by incurring everlasting punishment; their loss is the destruction of their greatest capital, the self, through wrongdoing and denial of Muhammad's signs.
rows.anchor: بأن استحقوا عذاب الأبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taḥrīm is preventing an act through proof that it must be avoided; its root is prohibition. Faḥishah denotes the ugliest major sins, and baghy is wrongful domination or seeking leadership by force.
rows.anchor: التحريم هو المنع من الفعل بإقامة الدليل على وجوب تجنبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The terms sultān, burhān, bayān, and furqān are related but differ: explanation clarifies meaning, proof establishes validity, criterion distinguishes it from confusion, and authority defeats its opposite.
rows.anchor: والسلطان والبرهان والبيان والفرقان نظائر وحدودها تختلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ummah is a community sharing one purpose; an appointed term is the set time when a period ends, after a span such as a debt, provision, promise, or lifespan.
rows.anchor: والأمة الجماعة التي يعمها معنى وأصلها من أمه يومه إذا قصده

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī and Abū Muslim take the prohibited fawāḥish, manifest and hidden, as all ugly acts and major sins; the verse then specifies sin, oppression, idolatry, and speaking about God without knowledge.
rows.anchor: أي جميع القبائح والكبائر عن الجبائي وأبي مسلم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the hidden immorality as fornication and the manifest one as nudity during circumambulation; another view distinguishes men's daytime and women's nighttime naked circumambulation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي الطواف فما ظهر منها طواف الرجال بالنهار

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī glosses sin as sins and disobedience; al-Farrāʾ says it means acts below the legal penalty, while al-Ḥasan says it is wine, supported by poetry using ithm for intoxicant.
rows.anchor: عن الجبائي. وقيل: الإثم ما دون الحد عن الفراء

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies sin as wine, supported by a poem cited by al-Akhfash.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الإثم الخمر عن الحسن وأنشد الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Innamā makes the statement exclusive: God prohibited the listed immoralities and related categories, not unspecified acts beyond them.
rows.anchor: لفظة إنما محققة لما ذكرنا فيه لما لم يذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase manifest and hidden means what is public and what is concealed.
rows.anchor: ما علن منها وما خفي وقد ذكرنا ما قيل فيه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies fornication as hidden immorality and nudity during circumambulation as its manifest form.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الفواحش هي الزنا وهو الذي بطن منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author summarizes the ugliness of the prohibited acts before detailing the categories in the following discussion.
rows.anchor: لما لم يذكر فذكر القبائح على الإجمال

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash cites two poems using ithm to mean wine, which clouds the mind and incurs sin.
rows.anchor: شربت الإثم حتى ضل عقلي كذاك الإثم يذهب بالعقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥasrah is grief over discovering that a wrong can no longer be repaired; tamyīz separates something from what does not belong with it, while rakm is piling things atop one another.
rows.anchor: الحسرة الغم بما انكشف من فوت استدراك الخطيئة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: One occasion says Abū Sufyān hired two thousand Abyssinian allies at Uḥud in addition to Arab support; Saʿīd b. Jubayr and Mujāhid relate this, and Kaʿb b. Mālik's verse describes their massed force.
rows.anchor: قيل نزلت في أبي سفيان بن حرب استأجر يوم أحد ألفين من الأحابيش

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Another occasion concerns twelve Qurashī providers at Badr, each supplying ten camels' worth of food per day; al-Kalbī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Muqātil list them and say al-ʿAbbās repented after defeat.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نزلت في المطعمين يوم بدر وكانوا اثني عشر رجلا

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq transmits that after Badr, Ṣafwān b. Umayya and ʿIkrima b. Abī Jahl persuaded merchants whose kin were killed to fund a new fight with the profits from the escaped caravan.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لما أصيبت قريش يوم بدر ورجع فلهم إلى مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelievers spend to fight the Messenger and believers and turn people from God's religion; even if they do not know it is God's religion, their actions objectively obstruct it.
rows.anchor: أموالهم } في قتال الرسول والمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their spending will become regret because they gain nothing from it in either world, then believers will defeat them; this forecast coming true supports the Prophet's truth.
rows.anchor: ثم ينكشف لهم ويظهر من ذلك الإنفاق ما يكون حسرة عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unbelievers who die in unbelief will be gathered to Hell; repeating “those who disbelieved” excludes some spenders who later accepted Islam from the afterlife threat.
rows.anchor: لأن جماعة ممن أنفقوا أسلموا بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of separating the bad from the good distinguishes unbelievers' spending from believers' spending, then piles all the unbelievers' expenditures together and punishes them in Hell as in 9:35.
rows.anchor: معناه ليميز الله نفقة الكافرين من نفقة المؤمنين

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says God distinguishes unbelievers from believers: in this world through victory, triumph, recognized names, and special rulings, and in the next through reward and Paradise.
rows.anchor: معناه ليميز الله الكافر من المؤمن في الدنيا بالغلبة والنصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation has the bad people piled atop one another in Hell, packed together like a heap of clouds; the phrase “make it in Hell” means He admits them there.
rows.anchor: ويجعل الخبيث بعضه على بعض في جهنم يضيقها عليهم فيركمه جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These people lose themselves because they traded spending their wealth in disobedience for punishment in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: قد خسروا أنفسهم لأنهم اشتروا بإنفاق الأموال في المعصية عذاب الله

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Ḥamza and Ḥafṣ read the verb about hearts inclining with yāʾ, as does al-Aʿmash; the other readers use tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة وحفص عن عاصم

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين
rows.claim: The common reading says the three were left behind; ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn, Abū Jaʿfar, and Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq read “they differed/opposed.”
rows.anchor: والقراءة المشهورة الذين خلفوا وقرأ علي بن الحسين زين العابدين ع

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima, Zirr b. Ḥubaysh, and ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd read the verb with a light consonant and fatḥa on khāʾ and lām, meaning left in the rear.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عكرمة وزر بن حبيش وعمرو بن عبيد خلفوا بفتح الخاء واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grammar of kāda can be explained by an implicit story clause, an implicit collective antecedent from the preceding context, or hearts as its subject; the choice affects whether the following verb is masculine or feminine.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: يجوز أن يكون فاعل كاد أحد ثلاثة أشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A feminine pronoun can take its agreement from the feminine plural noun in its explanatory clause, as the cited verse shows.
rows.anchor: فإذا هي شاخصة أبصار الذين كفروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khullifū means they were left behind and stayed; khālafū means they opposed and therefore stayed back.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ خلفوا فتأويله أقاموا ولم يبرحوا ومن قرأ خالفوا فمعناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zaygh is a heart's deviation from truth, like 61:5; the sun's decline and departure from a road also use this root. Takhليف means delaying something relative to those who have passed.
rows.anchor: الزيغ ميل القلب عن الحق ومنه قوله فلما زاغوا أزاغ الله قلوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth narrowing despite its breadth describes extreme remorse; ẓann here means certainty, as in Duraid b. al-Ṣimma's poem.
rows.anchor: ورحبت البلاد إذا اتسعت والرحب السعة ومنه مرحبا أي رحبت بلادك

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: The first verse was revealed about the Tabūk expedition and the hardship that nearly made some Muslims turn back; al-Ḥasan describes ten men sharing a camel and rationing moldy barley, old dates, and rancid fat, even sucking one date in turn.
rows.anchor: نزلت الآية الأولى في غزاة تبوك وما لحق المسلمين فيها من العسرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Khaythama delayed ten days, then left his comfortable shade, food, and two wives to join the Prophet; the Prophet welcomed him, and he is identified as the man whose heart had inclined to remain before God steadied him.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو خيثمة عبد الله بن خيثمة تخلف إلى أن مضى من مسير رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three are Kaʿb b. Mālik, Murāra b. al-Rabīʿ, and Hilāl b. Umayya, who stayed back from the expedition through laxity rather than hypocrisy, regretted it, and were shunned for fifty days until God accepted their repentance.
rows.anchor: نزلت في شأن كعب بن مالك ومرارة بن الربيع وهلال بن أمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath particle in “God has turned in mercy” signals a sworn assertion that He accepted the Prophet's and the believers' repentance and obedience; the Prophet is named as the opening and cause of their repentance.
rows.anchor: أقسم الله تعالى في هذه الآية لأن لام لقد لام القسم بأنه سبحانه قبل توبتهم

rows.speaker: علي بن موسى
rows.claim: A report from ʿAlī al-Riḍā gives an alternate reading: God's turning in mercy “by the Prophet” upon the Emigrants and Helpers.
rows.anchor: الرضا علي بن موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who followed the Prophet went with him to Tabūk during the time of hardship; sāʿah here means the period of hardship, not a literal hour.
rows.anchor: والمراد بساعة العسرة وقت العسرة لأن الساعة تقع على كل زمان

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jābir explains the hardship as scarcity of provisions, riding animals, and water.
rows.anchor: جابر: يعني عسرة الزاد وعسرة الظهر

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar says the believers faced severe heat and thirst, then God sent rain through the Prophet's supplication and they survived.
rows.anchor: عمر بن الخطاب: أصابنا حر شديد وعطش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group nearly inclined to abandon the expedition, but God restrained them and they continued; “then He turned to them” refers to mercy after that wavering, not apostasy from faith.
rows.anchor: فهموا بالانصراف من غزاتهم من غير أمر فعصمهم الله تعالى من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is compassionate to them because He overtook them with mercy; raʾfah is greater than raḥmah.
rows.anchor: رحيم تداركهم برحمته والرأفة أعظم من الرحمة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the three were left behind from acceptance of repentance after other people, including hypocrites, had been pardoned, like the group deferred to God's decision in 9:106.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: معناه خلفوا عن قبول التوبة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda say the three were left behind from the Tabūk campaign; the Ahl al-Bayt reading “opposed” means they acted contrary to the Prophet, and if they had merely been left behind they would not merit blame.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وقتادة معناه خلفوا عن غزوة تبوك لما تخلفوا هم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their world became constricted despite its breadth, describing the furthest degree of remorse; the Prophet had ordered people not to speak or sit with them while their repentance was delayed.
rows.anchor: ضاقت عليهم الأرض مع اتساعها وهذه صفة من بلغ غاية الندم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their ostracism was not a rejection of repentance: they were still commanded to repent, and God delayed revealing acceptance to intensify the trial and reform them and others against repeating the offense.
rows.anchor: ولم يكن ذلك على معنى رد توبتهم لأنهم كانوا مأمورين بالتوبة
